title: Crowns, bridges & veneers
blurb: Fixed prosthodontics from shade to fit: crowns, conventional and adhesive bridges, veneers and inlays, temporaries, lab prescriptions and disinfection.
question: You are assisting at a crown fit on 11. As the dentist seats the crown, saliva keeps seeping onto the prepared tooth, and later you notice the lab bag for the next case has no written prescription inside. What should you do in each situation?

teach.h: Fixed means the patient can't take it out
teach.body: Fixed prosthodontics covers restorations that are made outside the mouth (indirect) and then cemented or bonded in place for good. Crowns cover a whole tooth, veneers cover the front surface, inlays and onlays fit into or over a cavity, and bridges replace missing teeth by fixing to the teeth next to the gap. Most are made by a dental technician, working to the dentist's written prescription, over at least two visits.

root.label: Fixed (indirect) restorations
root.sub: Made outside the mouth, cemented in

children.label: Inlays & onlays
children.sub: Inside the cusps, or over them

teach.caption: Crowns can be metal, porcelain bonded to metal, or all-ceramic. Inlays and onlays can be gold, porcelain or composite.

teach.body: The false tooth filling the gap is the pontic. The teeth that hold the bridge up are the abutments, and the part fixed to each abutment is the retainer. A conventional bridge needs the abutments cut down for crowns, so it is strong but destructive. An adhesive (Maryland) bridge has a thin metal or ceramic wing bonded to the back of the neighbouring tooth, so little or no tooth is removed. A cantilever bridge is supported from one side only.

teach.caption: A three-unit bridge replacing 14: 13 and 15 are the abutments and 14 is the pontic. 21 has a single crown.

teach.h: A crown from start to finish

steps.label: Shade taken
steps.sub: Before prep, teeth moist, natural light

steps.label: Impressions & bite
steps.sub: Retraction cord, silicone or scan, opposing arch, bite record

steps.label: Temporary fitted
steps.sub: Made chairside, held with temporary cement

steps.label: Disinfect & prescribe
steps.sub: Disinfected, bagged, written prescription sent to lab

steps.label: Try-in & cement
steps.sub: Check fit, contacts, bite, shade; then cement

teach.caption: Veneers and inlays follow the same pattern. Some practices scan digitally instead of taking impressions.

teach.h: Your jobs at the fit appointment
items: Check the returned work is for the right patient and has been disinfected before it goes in the mouth.
Pass instruments to remove the temporary and clean off the old cement.
Have floss (contacts) and articulating paper (bite) ready for the try-in.
Isolate with cotton wool rolls and aspirate well so the tooth stays dry.
Mix the permanent cement to the manufacturer's ratio and timing, then load the fitting surface.
Help remove excess cement and pass floss between the teeth before the bite is checked again.

teach.h: Nothing goes to the lab undisinfected or unprescribed
teach.body: Impressions and appliances carry saliva and blood. Rinse under running water, disinfect with the practice's product for the full contact time, rinse again, then seal in a bag with the prescription in a separate pocket. Label it as disinfected and log it, so an audit can show every case was treated. The prescription is the dentist's formal written instruction: patient details, the work required, materials, shade and the return date. If any detail is missing, give it back to the dentist. Never fill it in yourself.

Job

Pushes the gum back to show the margin
Protects the prep until the fit
teach.caption: Take the shade at the start, before the prep. Teeth dry out during treatment and look lighter, which gives a false match.

rows.label: Job

Seals the final crown for good

teach.caption: Eugenol can stop resin cements setting properly, which is why eugenol-free temporary cement is often chosen before a bonded crown or veneer.

teach.text: If saliva keeps contaminating the tooth during cementation, don't add more cement or seat it quickly and say nothing. Improve the isolation and tell the dentist straight away: a wet tooth means a weak bond and a leaking seal. And a runny temporary cement that lets the temporary fall off points to the wrong mixing ratio.

items: Crowns cover the tooth, veneers the front, inlays sit in the cusps and onlays cover them.
Bridge: pontic replaces the tooth, abutments support it. Maryland bridges bond wings to the back of the neighbouring tooth.
Take the shade first, with the teeth moist and in natural light.
Disinfect, bag and send every case with a complete written prescription. Incomplete? Back to the dentist.
Dry field and the correct mixing ratio make or break cementation.

summary: You can now tell crowns, bridges, veneers, inlays and onlays apart, use the words pontic, abutment and retainer correctly, describe each stage from shade to cementation, and explain why every impression is disinfected and sent with a complete written prescription.

A.q: The dentist is about to prepare 21 for an all-ceramic crown. When is the best time to take the shade?
options: After the prep, once the tooth is dried
At the fit visit, just before cementing
Before the prep, with the teeth still moist
Under the operating light after the impression
A.why: Teeth dry out and look lighter during treatment, so the shade is taken first, with the teeth moist and ideally in natural light.

whyNot.0: A prepared, dried tooth looks paler than normal, so the shade would be wrong.
whyNot.1: By the fit visit the crown has already been made, so it is far too late to choose the shade.
whyNot.3: Teeth are dehydrated by then, and the operating light distorts colour.

A.q: Which description fits an adhesive (Maryland) bridge?
options: A pontic held by a wing bonded behind a neighbouring tooth
A pontic held by full crowns cemented on the teeth either side
A removable plate carrying a tooth, held on with wire clasps
A pontic screwed onto an abutment fixed into the jawbone
A.why: A Maryland bridge has a thin wing bonded to the palatal or lingual surface of the abutment, so little or no tooth needs removing.

whyNot.1: Full crowns on both abutments describe a conventional fixed-fixed bridge.
whyNot.2: A plate with clasps that the patient removes is a partial denture, not a bridge.
whyNot.3: A restoration screwed onto an abutment in the bone is an implant-retained restoration.

A.q: A lab bag for a bridge case is handed to you. The prescription has no shade or return date. What should you do?
options: Fill in the shade from the notes and initial it
Return it to the dentist to complete before sending
Send it and phone the missing details through later
Send it as it is and let the laboratory query it
A.why: The prescription is the dentist's written instruction, so only the dentist can complete it. Nothing goes to the lab until it is complete.

whyNot.0: You must not write clinical instructions on the dentist's behalf, even if the notes seem clear.
whyNot.2: Phoned details are easily misheard and leave no written record of what was prescribed.
whyNot.3: Sending an incomplete prescription risks the wrong work being made and delays the patient's treatment.

B.q: During cementation of a crown on 36, saliva repeatedly contaminates the prepared tooth. What is the best action?
options: Add extra cement to make up for the moisture
Seat the crown quickly before the cement sets
Improve isolation and tell the dentist at once
Dry only the inside of the crown and carry on
B.why: Moisture weakens the cement bond and seal, so the field must be dried and the dentist must know before the crown is seated.

whyNot.0: More cement does not fix contamination; it just leaves more excess to remove.
whyNot.1: Rushing seats the crown on a wet tooth, giving a poor seal that may leak or fail.
whyNot.3: Drying the crown alone leaves the contaminated tooth surface, and the dentist is not told.

B.q: A bridge replaces a missing 24. What is the replacement tooth in the bridge called?
options: The abutment
The retainer
The connector
The pontic
B.why: The pontic is the false tooth that fills the gap in a bridge.

whyNot.0: Abutments are the natural teeth (or implants) that support the bridge.
whyNot.1: A retainer is the part of the bridge that fixes to each abutment.
whyNot.2: A connector joins the pontic to the retainer; it is not the replacement tooth.

B.q: A crown impression is ready to go to the laboratory. Which sequence is correct?
options: Disinfect, bag, then rinse just before collection
Rinse, disinfect for the full time, rinse, then bag
Bag it straight away and let the lab disinfect it
Dry it with air, wrap in paper towel, then bag it
B.why: Rinsing first removes saliva and blood so the disinfectant can work; a final rinse removes disinfectant before it is sealed and labelled.

whyNot.0: The impression must be rinsed before disinfecting, and it should be sealed once treated, not opened again.
whyNot.2: Sending an undisinfected impression puts laboratory staff at risk of infection.
whyNot.3: Drying and wrapping does not disinfect, and paper towel can stick to or distort the impression.

C.q: A temporary crown falls off the day after it was fitted. The nurse remembers the temporary cement looked thin and runny. What is the most likely cause?
options: The shade was poorly matched
The margin was polished too much
The bite was perfectly balanced
The mixing ratio was incorrect
C.why: A thin, runny mix usually means the wrong ratio of components, which gives a weak cement that lets the temporary dislodge.

whyNot.0: Shade affects appearance only, not how well the cement holds.
whyNot.1: Polishing does not explain why the cement itself looked runny.
whyNot.2: A balanced bite helps a temporary stay on rather than come off.

options: A thin facing bonded to the front of a tooth
A full crown covering the whole tooth
A cast filling fitted inside the cusps
A metal wing bonded to a tooth's palatal side
C.why: A veneer is a thin layer of porcelain or composite bonded to the labial surface, usually to improve shape or colour.

whyNot.1: A full crown covers all surfaces, not just the front.
whyNot.2: A cast filling fitted within the cusps is an inlay.
whyNot.3: A metal wing bonded palatally is the retainer of an adhesive (Maryland) bridge.

C.q: Which check is NOT part of trying in a new crown before it is cemented?
options: Contact points with floss
The bite with articulating paper
The margins and fit on the tooth
Pulp vitality with an electric tester
C.why: Vitality testing is a diagnostic investigation, not part of a crown try-in. At try-in the dentist checks fit, contacts, bite and shade.

whyNot.0: Floss checks the crown touches the neighbouring teeth correctly.
whyNot.1: Articulating paper shows whether the crown is high in the bite.
whyNot.2: The margins must fit closely so the crown seals and doesn't trap plaque.

reteach.title: Think of a bridge like a real bridge
reteach.question: Picture a road bridge over a river. Which part of a dental bridge is the road over the water, and which parts are the pillars on each bank?

blocks.body: The gap is the river. The pillars on each bank are the abutment teeth, and they carry all the load. The road over the water is the pontic. Where the road joins each pillar is the retainer. A conventional bridge builds a big concrete collar (a crown) round each pillar. A Maryland bridge just glues a bracket to the back of one pillar, which is gentler but less strong.

blocks.text: Pontic = the false tooth. Abutment = the supporting tooth. If you're stuck, remember the abutment 'butts up' to the gap and holds it.

explain.body: A crown covers the whole tooth, often after a large filling or root canal treatment. A veneer is a thin facing on the front. An inlay sits within the cusps of a back tooth; an onlay extends over one or more cusps.

test.q: A gold restoration covers two cusps of a lower molar. What is it called?
options: An inlay
An onlay
A veneer
A pontic
test.why: An onlay extends over one or more cusps; an inlay stays within them.

whyNot.0: An inlay sits inside the cusps and doesn't cover them.
whyNot.2: A veneer is a facing on the front of a tooth.
whyNot.3: A pontic is the false tooth in a bridge.

explain.body: A bridge replaces missing teeth by fixing to the teeth next to the gap. The pontic is the false tooth, the abutments support it. Conventional bridges crown the abutments; adhesive (Maryland) bridges bond a wing to the back of a neighbour.

explain.caption: 45 and 47 are abutments; 46 is the pontic.

test.q: Which bridge needs the least removal of tooth tissue?
options: A conventional fixed-fixed bridge
A conventional cantilever bridge
An adhesive (Maryland) bridge
A bridge with two full crowns
test.why: A Maryland bridge bonds a wing to the back of the abutment, so little or no tooth is cut away.

whyNot.0: Fixed-fixed bridges crown both abutments, removing a lot of tooth.
whyNot.1: A conventional cantilever still crowns its abutment.
whyNot.3: Two full crowns means two teeth are cut down.

explain.body: Shade first, then the dentist prepares the tooth, places retraction cord, takes the impression, the opposing impression and a bite record, then makes and fits a temporary crown with temporary cement.

test.q: Why is a temporary crown fitted after the prep?
options: To protect the tooth and keep its position
To record the shade for the laboratory
To test the strength of the permanent cement
To let the gum recede before the fit visit
test.why: A temporary protects the prepared tooth from sensitivity and damage and stops neighbouring and opposing teeth drifting into the space.

whyNot.1: The shade is recorded with a shade guide, not a temporary.
whyNot.2: The temporary uses temporary cement and has nothing to do with testing permanent cement.
whyNot.3: Gum recession is not wanted; a good temporary keeps the gum healthy.

explain.body: Rinse, disinfect for the full contact time, rinse, bag and label as disinfected, with the prescription in a separate pocket. The prescription comes from the dentist and must be complete. Returned work is disinfected again before it is tried in.

test.q: Why should the practice log that each lab case was disinfected?
options: So the laboratory can charge less
So the shade can be checked later
So an audit can show it was always done
So the dentist can sign the prescription
test.why: A written log is evidence for infection control audits and inspections that every case was disinfected before leaving the surgery.

whyNot.0: Lab fees are not linked to the disinfection log.
whyNot.1: The shade is on the prescription, not the disinfection log.
whyNot.3: The dentist signs the prescription itself, not a disinfection log.
